items.title: Frank Foster — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: In the trumpet section were Joe Newman... I said Joe Newman, right? ... We all knew how to act. ... Every now and then Joe Newman would get on me for lateness.

ctx.x: When you joined the band who was there at that point?

In the trumpet section were Joe Newman, a gentleman by the name of Paul Campbell -- they used to call him Uncle Cam -- Wendell Culley, a very distinguished looking and acting person from Worchester, Mass., who spoke perfect English and was a gentleman and always wore a suit and tie. I said Joe Newman, right? The lead trumpeter was a person called Renauld Jones. Trombones were Henry Coker, Benny Powell, and the composer-arranger Johnny Mandel. The saxophones were Marshall Royal, Frank Wess, Ernie Wilkins, Charlie…
So at that point Jimmy Wilkins had left the band?

items.title: Frank Foster interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 7, 1998
items.q: Joe Newman was instrumental in getting me a lot of gigs, a lot of work around town, and on a few recordings

ctx.x: Sixteen bars here, sixteen bars there.

Yeah, yeah. And the fact of not getting to play a ballad, and wanting to play a ballad, that really ate me up, because I was of the mind then, well if you’d just give me a chance I’ll learn, I’ll get better. But not to have a chance at all. But don’t misunderstand, there was no animosity toward Mr. Basie. There was just this gnawing desire to be in a situation where I could get to play more. I wanted to play more, and so for family reasons and musical reasons, I wanted to get out. Plus, some of the most exciting…
level. Even personally they weren’t as much fun to be around. And not only did they not play as well.

items.title: Frank Foster and Bill Hughes interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, Schenectady, New York, March 28, 1995
items.q: Joe and Sonny were two of the most colorful characters in the band... there was Joe Newman

ctx.x: And there we were, two of the, you know—

And Joe and Sonny were two of the most colorful characters in the band, which was full of colorful characters. Everybody had a story. And then when we acquired the likes of Snooky Young to play lead trumpet, and there was Joe Newman and —
